units.title: Modals & semi-modals
units.intro: Modals (*can, must, should, might…*) express ability, obligation, advice and possibility without *to*.

cards.title: Core modals
rule: **must / have to** = obligation; **should / ought to** = advice.
**can / could** = ability or permission; **may / might** = possibility.

cards.title: Choosing a modal by meaning
body: Modals add attitude to a verb. Always ask *what is the speaker's meaning?* – **obligation** (must, have to), **no obligation** (don't have to, needn't), **prohibition** (mustn't), **advice** (should, ought to), **ability** (can, could), **permission** (can, may), **possibility** (may, might, could).
**must** usually shows the speaker's own feeling or a rule; **have to** often shows an outside rule: *I must study tonight* vs *We have to wear uniform.* In the past both become **had to**.
Grammar of modals: no -s (*she can*), no to (*you should go*), questions by inversion (*Can you help?*), negatives with not (*mustn't, can't*).

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "You should to revise tonight."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** **must / have to** = obligation; **should / ought to** = advice.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "You should to revise tonight." breaks this rule.
**Check:** **can / could** = ability or permission; **may / might** = possibility.

cards.title: Step by step: Core modals
body: **Step 1:** Modals (can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would) are followed by the bare infinitive: "She must go" (not "must to go" or "must goes").
**Step 2:** Choose by meaning: ability (can, could), permission (can, may, could), possibility (may, might, could), obligation (must, have to), advice (should, ought to), prohibition (mustn't).
**Step 3:** "Mustn't" = it is forbidden; "don't have to / needn't" = it is not necessary.
**Step 4:** Past forms: could (past ability), had to (past obligation); speculation about the past uses modal + have + V3: "He must have left."
**Step 5:** Modals never take -s and form questions/negatives without "do": "Can you swim?", "You should not shout."

**Example:** "You ___ wear a uniform; it's optional." → "don't have to" (no obligation). "You ___ smoke in the laboratory." → "mustn't" (prohibition). "She ___ have taken the bus; her car is here." → "must" (logical certainty about the past).

cards.title: Mnemonic — "A-P-P-O-A"
body: Ability, Permission, Possibility, Obligation, Advice: name the meaning first, then pick the modal.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: The favourite exam trap is mustn't vs don't have to. Ask: is it forbidden (mustn't) or just unnecessary (don't have to)?

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Almaz might be working late tonight.

options.A: Definitely, she will be working late tonight.
options.B: Certainly, she will be working late tonight.
options.C: She is unlikely to work late tonight.
options.D: Perhaps she will be working late tonight.
options.E: She will never be working late tonight.

cards.why:
**Meaning:** The modal verb **might** expresses a possibility, not a certainty. 
**Step 1:** Choices A and B imply 100% certainty (Definitely/Certainly), which is wrong.
**Step 2:** Choices C and E imply it won't happen, which is wrong.
**Step 3:** Choice D uses "Perhaps" (ምናልባት), which is the correct synonym for 'might'.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q:
Elsa: Do you have to go to the party now? 
Abraham: I _______ go but I don’t think I will.
cards.why: The speaker says 'I don't think I will', which indicates uncertainty or a weak possibility. 'Might' is used to express a weak possibility that something will happen.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: All the students _______ take Model Examinations this week. They won’t be given later on.
cards.why: The second sentence ('They won’t be given later on') implies a strict requirement or obligation. 'Must' is used to express strong obligation.

cards.title: Perfect modals
rule: **must have + V3** = logical conclusion about the past.
**could have + V3** = past possibility that did not happen.

cards.title: Perfect modals in context
body: Perfect modals look back at the past: **modal + have + past participle**.
**must have** = I'm sure it happened (*The streets are wet – it must have rained*). **can't/couldn't have** = I'm sure it didn't happen. **may/might/could have** = perhaps it happened.
**should have** = it was the right thing but it didn't happen (regret or criticism): *You should have revised.* **shouldn't have** = it happened, but it was wrong.
**could have** can also mean a chance that was not taken: *We could have won if we had trained.* **needn't have** = done, but unnecessary.

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "She must left early."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** **must have + V3** = logical conclusion about the past.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "She must left early." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "She must have left early."

cards.title: Memory tip
body: After a modal use the bare infinitive: must go, not must to go.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Choose the modal for meaning (obligation vs advice vs possibility) and keep the bare verb after it.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Every child should __________ his or her parents and other people.
cards.why: **Rule:** After modal verbs like *should, must, can, could, will,* we always use the **bare infinitive** (base form of the verb without 'to'). Therefore, "should respect" is correct.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: It is so amazing how a single tower can ___19___ so astonishing.
cards.why: After the modal verb 'can', the base form of the verb (without 'to' or '-s') must be used. Therefore, 'look' is correct.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: "The window is broken and there is a football on the floor. Someone ____ it."
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The evidence makes the speaker sure about a past event.

**Step 2:** Strong deduction about the past: must have + past participle.

**Step 3:** "should have" would mean it was the right thing to do.

**Tip:** Choose the modal by meaning: obligation, advice, ability, permission, possibility or deduction. For the past, use modal + have + past participle.

glossary.meaning: helping verb of mood: can, must, should…

tips.text: After a modal use the bare infinitive: must go, not must to go.

questions.q: I failed the national biology matriculation exam; I ________ harder instead of wasting my time on social media.
questions.label: 1. I failed the national biology matriculation exam; I ________

similar.q: I failed the national biology matriculation exam;
According to the laboratory safety rules, you ____

why: Answer B: should have studied
Analyze the grammatical structure

The context 'I failed...; I [blank] harder' indicates a past regret or criticism of an action that was advisable but did not happen. This requires the past regret modal structure ($$\text{should have} + \text{V}_3$$).
Identify the matriculation trap

Students often confuse 'must have studied' (logical deduction of fact) with 'should have studied' (regret). Option A implies the speaker is deducing that they studied, which contradicts 'I failed'. Option B is correct because it expresses regret.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.q: According to the laboratory safety rules, you ________ enter the chemistry room without wearing safety goggles.
questions.label: 2. According to the laboratory safety rules, you ________ enter

similar.q: According to the laboratory safety rules, you ____
Aster has been studying and living in London for t

why: Answer B: must not
Analyze the grammatical structure
The context describes a strict laboratory safety rule. This requires a modal of prohibition to show the action is forbidden ($$\text{must not} + \text{V}_{\text{base}}$$).
Identify the matriculation trap

Students often confuse 'don't have to' (lack of obligation/optional) with 'must not' (prohibition/forbidden). Option A would incorrectly imply that wearing goggles is optional, which violates safety rules. Option B is correct.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

The soccer field is completely covered in puddles;

why: Answer A: must
Analyze the grammatical structure
The context presents strong present evidence ('living in London for ten years'). This requires a modal of present logical deduction to show high certainty ($$\text{must} + \text{V}_{\text{base}}$$).
Identify the matriculation trap
Students sometimes choose 'must have' (Option D), but 'must have' is for past deduction ($$\text{must have} + \text{V}_3$$) and cannot be followed by the base verb 'speak'. Option A is correct.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.label: 4. The soccer field is completely covered in puddles; it ______

similar.q: The soccer field is completely covered in puddles;
The main classroom door was heavily jammed, but th

why: Answer B: must have rained
Analyze the grammatical structure
The present evidence 'The soccer field is completely covered in puddles' leads to a strong positive deduction about a past event. This requires 'must have' ($$\text{must have} + \text{V}_3$$).
Identify the matriculation trap

Students often confuse 'should have rained' (past regret/unrealized advice) with 'must have rained' (past deduction of fact). Option A is incorrect because we are deducing a fact based on physical evidence, making Option B correct.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.q: The main classroom door was heavily jammed, but the strong security guard ________ open it for us.
questions.label: 5. The main classroom door was heavily jammed, but the strong s

similar.q: The main classroom door was heavily jammed, but th
Tomorrow is a national public holiday, so we _____

why: Answer B: was able to
Analyze the grammatical structure
This sentence describes a specific, successful action in a past situation. This requires 'was able to' or 'managed to' ($$\text{Subject} + \text{was/were able to} + \text{V}_{\text{base}}$$).
Identify the matriculation trap

Students often choose 'could' (Option A) because they translate it as past ability. However, 'could' is only used for general past ability, while specific past successes require 'was able to' (Option B).
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.q: Tomorrow is a national public holiday, so we ________ wake up early to attend classes.
questions.label: 6. Tomorrow is a national public holiday, so we ________ wake u

similar.q: Tomorrow is a national public holiday, so we _____
I failed the national biology matriculation exam;

why: Answer B: don't have to
Analyze the grammatical structure

The context describes a lack of obligation or necessity because tomorrow is a holiday (it is optional to wake up early). This requires 'don't have to' ($$\text{don't have to} + \text{V}_{\text{base}}$$).
Identify the matriculation trap
Students often choose 'must not' (Option A) because they confuse prohibition with a lack of obligation. Option B is correct because waking up early is not forbidden; it is simply not required.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.q: The river water was contaminated with waste; we ________ drunk it without boiling it first.
questions.label: 7. The river water was contaminated with waste; we ________ dru

similar.q: I failed the national biology matriculation exam;

why: Answer B: shouldn't have
Analyze the grammatical structure

The context 'The river water was contaminated... we [blank] drunk it' indicates a past criticism or regret of an action that did happen but was undesirable. This requires 'shouldn't have' ($$\text{shouldn't have} + \text{V}_3$$).
Identify the matriculation trap
Option A 'must not have' is grammatically incorrect for past logical deduction or regret in standard English. Option B is correct because it expresses regret for a completed past action.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.q: He ________ stolen the library books yesterday; he was with me in the seminar hall all afternoon.
questions.label: 8. He ________ stolen the library books yesterday; he was with

similar.q: According to the laboratory safety rules, you ____

why: Answer B: can't have
Analyze the grammatical structure
The context provides strong negative evidence ('he was with me... all afternoon'). This requires a modal of past logical deduction to show negative certainty ($$\text{can't have} + \text{V}_3$$).
Identify the matriculation trap

Students often try to use 'must not have' to show negative certainty, which is incorrect. In English, 'can't have' (Option B) is the correct past negative equivalent of 'must have' to show that a past action was impossible.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.q: Every student should ________ to the lecture hall on time to secure a seat.
questions.label: 9. Every student should ________ to the lecture hall on time to

similar.q: Aster has been studying and living in London for t

why: Answer C: come
Analyze the grammatical structure
Core modal verbs like 'should' must strictly be followed by a bare infinitive verb ($$\text{Modal} + \text{V}_{\text{base}}$$).
Identify the matriculation trap

Students often make the error of inserting 'to' after 'should', choosing 'to come' (Option A), or adding participle suffixes, choosing 'coming' (Option B). Only the bare infinitive 'come' (Option C) is correct.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.q: You have a severe cough; you ________ see the doctor before your condition gets worse.
questions.label: 10. You have a severe cough; you ________ see the doctor before

similar.q: The soccer field is completely covered in puddles;

why: Answer A: had better
Analyze the grammatical structure

The context describes strong, urgent advice with a negative consequence if ignored ('before your condition gets worse'). This requires the semi-modal 'had better' ($$\text{had better} + \text{V}_{\text{base}}$$).
Identify the matriculation trap
Option C 'ought' is incorrect because it lacks 'to'. Option D 'have to' shows external obligation but is less natural for urgent, cautionary advice. Option A is correct.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

Eyob: “Do you have to go to the cinema now?”

similar.a: You should drink warm water / see a doctor.

why: Answer D: should
The speaker is giving advice.
Advice is expressed with should / ought to.
"must not" forbids; "can't" denies possibility; "needn't" says it isn't necessary.

questions.q: He ____ have left already; his bag is still here.
questions.label: 14. He ____ have left already; his bag is still here.

similar.q: Complete: The ground is wet. It ____ have rained.
Complete: She ____ have seen me; she was asleep.

why: Answer C: can't
The bag is still here, so the speaker is sure he has not left.
Negative deduction about the past: can't have + past participle.
"must have" would mean the opposite.
questions.tip: Choose the modal by meaning: obligation, advice, ability, permission, possibility or deduction. For the past, use modal + have + past participle.

Complete: We ____ (not / eat) so much.

questions.q: Correct the error: "She must has forgotten the meeting."
questions.label: 16. Correct the error: "She must has forgotten the meeting."

similar.q: Correct: He should has called.
Correct: They might has lost.

questions.answer: She must have forgotten the meeting.

Perfect modal: modal + have + past participle.
So: must have forgotten.

"could have + past participle" describes a past possibility that was not used.
They did not take the coastal road because nobody told them.

questions.q: True or false: "You needn't have bought bread" means you bought bread but it wasn't necessary.
questions.label: 20. True or false: "You needn't have bought bread" means you bought bread but it wasn't necessary.

similar.q: Meaning: "You didn't need to come."
similar.a: It wasn't necessary to come (you probably didn't).

similar.q: Meaning: "You needn't have come."
similar.a: You came, but it wasn't necessary.

why: True. needn't have + past participle = the action was done, but it was unnecessary.
Compare "didn't need to buy" which usually means it wasn't done.
So the statement is true.
questions.tip: Choose the modal by meaning: obligation, advice, ability, permission, possibility or deduction. For the past, use modal + have + past participle.
